name: Ezekiel
v: The word of the LORD hit me hard:

"Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy. Tell them — this is what the Lord GOD says: Doom to the shepherds of Israel who only feed themselves. Shouldn't shepherds feed the flock?
You eat the fat. You wear the wool. You butcher the prime animals. But the flock — you don't feed.

The weak, you haven't strengthened. The sick, you haven't healed. The wounded, you haven't bandaged. The strays, you haven't brought back. The lost, you haven't searched for. You've ruled them with brute force and cruelty.
So they scattered — no shepherd anywhere — and became food for every wild thing that prowls. Scattered.
My sheep wandered across every mountain, every high hill. They were dispersed over the whole face of the earth, and no one looked for them. No one searched.
So listen, shepherds. Listen to the word of the LORD:

As I live — declares the Lord GOD — because my flock has been plundered, because my flock has become prey for every wild beast since there was no shepherd, because my shepherds didn't search for my flock but fed themselves instead and let the flock starve —
therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the LORD.

This is what the Lord GOD says: I am against the shepherds. I will demand my flock from their hand. I am ending their shepherding career. They will not feed themselves anymore. I will pull my sheep out of their mouths — they will not be food for them any longer.
Because this is what the Lord GOD says: Look — I myself will search for my sheep. I will find them.

As a shepherd looks for his scattered flock on the day he's among them, that's how I will look for my sheep. I will rescue them from every place they were scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness.

I will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the countries, lead them home to their own soil. I will graze them on the mountains of Israel, by the streams, in every inhabited place of the land.
I will feed them in good pasture. The high mountains of Israel will be their grazing ground. There they'll lie down in fine pasture, feeding on rich grass on the mountains of Israel.
I will shepherd my flock myself. I will make them lie down. This is the word of the Lord GOD.
I will search for the lost. I will bring back the strays. I will bandage the broken. I will strengthen the sick. But the sleek and the strong — I will destroy. I will shepherd with justice.
As for you, my flock — this is what the Lord GOD says: I am about to judge between one sheep and another, between rams and goats.
Isn't it enough that you feed in good pasture? Do you have to trample the rest with your feet? You drink clear water — do you have to muddy what's left with your hooves?
So my flock has to feed on what your feet have trampled and drink what your feet have fouled?
Therefore the Lord GOD says to them: Look — I myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean.
Because you shoulder and shove and ram the weak ones with your horns until you've scattered them everywhere —
I will rescue my flock. They will not be prey anymore. I will judge between one sheep and another.
I will raise up one shepherd over them — my servant David. He will feed them. He will be their shepherd.
I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David will be prince among them. I, the LORD, have spoken.
I will cut a covenant of peace with them. I will clear the wild beasts out of the land, so they can sleep safely in the wilderness and in the forests.
I will make them and the places around my hill a blessing. I will send the rains in their season — showers of blessing falling.

The trees of the field will yield their fruit, the land will yield its harvest, and they will live secure on their own soil. They will know I am the LORD when I shatter the bars of their yoke and rescue them from the hand of those who enslaved them.
They will not be plunder for the nations anymore. Wild animals will not devour them. They will live in safety, and no one will make them afraid.
I will raise up for them a garden of renown. No more will they be swept away by famine in the land. No more will they bear the contempt of the nations.
They will know that I, the LORD their God, am with them, and that they — the house of Israel — are my people. This is the word of the Lord GOD.
You are my flock, the flock of my pasture. You are human. I am your God. This is the word of the Lord GOD."

com.d:
# Ezekiel 34: The Shepherd's Heart

God's deepest complaint against Israel's leaders is not their outright rebellion but their negligence—they have become shepherds who care nothing for the flock. In this powerful indictment, the Lord reveals His tender passion for people who have been abandoned, scattered, and left vulnerable to predators. The passage unfolds God's heart: He grieves over shepherds who feed themselves instead of feeding the sheep, and He promises to step in personally where human leaders have failed.

The image of sheep without a shepherd captures something true about our world. People are genuinely lost—not necessarily because they've chosen darkness, but because those entrusted to guide them have been indifferent. Sick sheep go unhealed. The lost are never searched for. The strong dominate the weak. This was Israel's tragic reality, and it remains a challenge whenever leaders prioritize their own comfort, reputation, or advancement over the wellbeing of those they serve.

What makes this passage breathtaking is that God doesn't simply execute judgment—He becomes the Shepherd Himself. He will seek out His scattered sheep, gather them from all the places they've been driven, and lead them to good pasture. This isn't distant, administrative care; it's intimate, hands-on tending. God will feed them, strengthen them, and establish a covenant of peace. Most remarkably, in verse 24, God promises to raise up "David my servant"—a messianic promise pointing to Jesus, who embodies the faithful Shepherd.

For those who have felt abandoned or neglected, Ezekiel 34 offers profound assurance: you have not been forgotten. Your true Shepherd knows you by name and will pursue you with relentless love. For those in leadership—in church, family, or community—this passage calls us to humility and sacrifice, remembering that we shepherd on behalf of the Good Shepherd Himself.

What areas of your life do you need the Shepherd's personal care and restoration? Bring that need to Him now.
com.s:
Ezekiel 34 stands as one of the most theologically significant shepherd discourses in the Hebrew Bible, composed during the Babylonian exile when the prophet addressed the displaced Judean community regarding the failures of their former leadership and the promise of divine restoration. The chapter divides naturally into two movements: an indictment against Israel's shepherds (vv. 1-10) and an extended promise of Yahweh's direct shepherding intervention (vv. 11-31). The shepherd metaphor for kingship was ubiquitous throughout the ancient Near East, appearing in Mesopotamian royal inscriptions and Egyptian literature, making Ezekiel's appropriation of this imagery both politically charged and culturally resonant for his audience.

The Hebrew term *rō'îm* (shepherds) functions throughout as a transparent cipher for the Davidic kings and ruling elite whose mismanagement precipitated national catastrophe. The prophetic accusation centers on their self-enrichment at the expense of the flock, employing the verb *rā'āh* (to shepherd/feed) with bitter irony—these shepherds have fed themselves rather than the sheep. Particularly striking is the description of the neglected sheep as *hanniphrāṣôt* (the scattered ones), a term carrying connotations of violent dispersion that captures the trauma of exile itself.

The theological pivot occurs in verse 11 with Yahweh's dramatic self-insertion as Israel's true shepherd, a motif later developed extensively in Johannine Christology. This divine shepherding encompasses gathering, feeding, healing, and judging between sheep—notably distinguishing between fat sheep and lean, between rams and goats, suggesting internal social stratification requiring divine adjudication. The promise of "one shepherd, my servant David" (v. 23) has generated substantial interpretive discussion regarding whether this indicates a restored Davidic monarchy or an idealized messianic figure transcending historical kingship.

The chapter concludes with covenant renewal language, promising the *bərît šālôm* (covenant of peace) that transforms the very landscape into paradisiacal abundance. This eschatological vision integrates themes of security, fertility, and divine presence that recur throughout Ezekiel's restoration oracles. The passage fundamentally reconceptualizes political theology by subordinating human governance to divine sovereignty while simultaneously promising renewed Davidic leadership under Yahweh's ultimate rule—a tension that would prove generative for later Jewish and Christian messianic reflection.
com.p:
This prophecy came through Ezekiel approximately 585 years before the birth of Christ, delivered during the darkest chapter of Israel's history—the Babylonian exile. The temple lay in ruins, Jerusalem was devastated, and God's people languished in a foreign land. Within the grand redemptive arc, this passage emerges from the ashes of the failed monarchy, when the shepherds God had appointed over Israel had utterly betrayed their sacred trust, scattering the flock rather than gathering it.

The indictment opens with devastating precision against the shepherds of Israel—the kings, priests, and prophets who fed themselves rather than the sheep. They consumed the fat, clothed themselves with wool, and slaughtered the choice animals while leaving the weak unstrengthened, the sick unhealed, the injured unbandaged, the strayed unreturned, and the lost unsought. This is not merely political critique but covenantal prosecution. Because of their failure, the sheep were scattered across every mountain and hill, becoming food for wild beasts—a portrait of Israel dispersed among the nations.

Yet from this judgment rises one of Scripture's most radiant messianic promises. The LORD Himself declares: "I Myself will search for My sheep and seek them out." Here prophecy leaps across centuries toward Bethlehem. The Good Shepherd whom Jesus claimed to be in John 10 is no new figure—He is the One promised here, the divine Shepherd who leaves heaven's glory to seek the lost sheep of Israel. When Christ said, "I am the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep," He was announcing that Ezekiel 34 had found its fulfillment in His own flesh.

The prophecy then unveils "My servant David," a single shepherd to tend them. This cannot mean the historical David, dead for centuries, but David's greater Son—the Messiah who unites the offices of king and shepherd in one person. The covenant of peace promised here, where dangerous beasts are removed and showers of blessing fall, began its inauguration at Christ's first coming and awaits its consummation when He returns.

For the church dwelling between the advents, this chapter speaks both comfort and calling. Christ has gathered us as His flock, binding our wounds and strengthening our weakness. Yet we await the day when every scattered sheep hears His voice, when the final harvest is complete, and when the everlasting covenant of peace transforms all creation into pastures of perfect shalom.
